title: Ceyx et Alcyone. Somnus
titleEn: The House of Sleep and the Halcyons — Metamorphoses XI.583–748
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Juno will not be petitioned any longer on behalf of a dead man, and sends Iris to the house of Sleep to have the truth carried to Alcyone in a dream. Sleep wakes Morpheus out of his thousand sons; he takes the drowned shape of Ceyx and stands at her bed, and she wakes to an empty room and mourns. In the morning she goes down to the shore, watches a body carried in by the waves, and knows it. Both are changed into birds, and for seven calm days of winter Aeolus holds the winds in while she broods on the sea.

sentences.t:
At dea non ultra pro functo morte rogari
sustinet;
sentences.l: But the goddess does not bear to be entreated any longer on behalf of one who is done with death;
sentences.i: But the goddess could bear no longer to be petitioned for a man already finished with dying;
sentences.n: The goddess is Juno, named only at 629. functo morte is the participle of defungor, “to discharge, have done with”: Ceyx has already got his dying over, so Alcyone's prayers for his return are prayers for a dead man. rogari is a passive infinitive after sustinet, “to be asked”, and pro functo names the person the asking is for.

sentences.t:
utque manus funestas arceat aris,
“Iri, meae” dixit “fidissima nuntia vocis,
vise soporiferam Somni velociter aulam
exstinctique iube Ceycis imagine mittat
somnia ad Alcyonen veros narrantia casus.”
sentences.l: and so that she might keep hands defiled by death away from her altars, “Iris,” she said, “most faithful messenger of my voice, go swiftly and visit the sleep-bringing hall of Sleep, and bid him send to Alcyone, in the likeness of dead Ceyx, dreams that tell the true events.”
sentences.i: and to keep hands fouled by a death away from her altars she said, “Iris, truest carrier of my voice, go quickly to the drowsy hall of Sleep and tell him to send Alcyone dreams that will report what really happened, wearing the shape of Ceyx now dead.”
sentences.n: funestas is a technical word: contact with a death made a household polluted, and Alcyone, praying for a husband who is already drowned, defiles Juno's altar without knowing it. That, and not pity, is what moves the goddess. iube ... mittat puts the ordered verb straight into the subjunctive with no ut, so that the command is given in one clause; imagine is ablative of the shape the dreams are to wear.

sentences.t:
Dixerat: induitur velamina mille colorum
Iris, et arcuato caelum curvamine signans
tecta petit iussi sub nube latentia regis.
sentences.l: She had spoken: Iris puts on garments of a thousand colours, and, marking the sky with an arched bending, makes for the roof of the bidden king, hidden beneath its cloud.
sentences.i: She had spoken. Iris dressed herself in her thousand-coloured robe, signed the sky with her arch, and made for the house of the king she was sent to command, where it lies hidden under cloud.
sentences.n: induitur takes the accusative velamina: the passive is used in a middle sense, “she clothes herself in”, and English needs a reflexive to say it. arcuato curvamine, “with an arched bending”, is the rainbow's track, which she will travel back along at 632. iussi regis is a compressed participle — the king who has been given the order, that is Sleep, whose hall Juno named at 586.

sentences.t:
Est prope Cimmerios longo spelunca recessu,
mons cavus, ignavi domus et penetralia Somni:
sentences.l: There is near the Cimmerians a cave with a long recess, a hollow mountain, the house and inner chambers of idle Sleep:
sentences.i: Near the Cimmerians there is a cave in a deep recess, a hollowed mountain, the home and the inmost rooms of listless Sleep:
sentences.n: Est prope ... is the existential opening that sets a place down before the story walks into it. penetralia is the innermost part of a house, the room a stranger never reaches; with domus it gives Sleep a proper dwelling rather than a hole in a hill. ignavi is “without energy, doing nothing”, not “cowardly”.

sentences.t:
quo numquam radiis oriens mediusve cadensve
Phoebus adire potest.
sentences.l: whither Phoebus can never approach with his rays, whether rising or in mid-course or falling.
sentences.i: where Phoebus can never reach with his rays, rising, at noon, or going down.
sentences.n: quo is the relative adverb, “to which place”. The three words oriens, mediusve cadensve cover the whole day between them — sunrise, noon, sunset — and the doubled -ve is “either ... or”; medius is a plain adjective standing between two participles and doing their work.

sentences.t:
Nebulae caligine mixtae
exhalantur humo dubiaeque crepuscula lucis.
sentences.l: Mists mingled with gloom are breathed out from the ground, and twilights of uncertain light.
sentences.i: Fogs mixed with darkness steam up out of the earth, and half-lights of a doubtful day.
sentences.n: exhalantur is passive, with humo a bare ablative of source: the ground breathes them out. crepuscula is a second subject of the same verb, and it is plural — not one dusk but a standing supply of them. dubiae ... lucis is a genitive of description wrapped round it.

sentences.t:
Non vigil ales ibi cristati cantibus oris
evocat auroram, nec voce silentia rumpunt
sollicitive canes canibusve sagacior anser.
sentences.l: No wakeful bird calls forth the dawn there with the crowings of its crested mouth, nor do anxious dogs break the silences with their voice, or the goose, keener than dogs.
sentences.i: No cockerel there crows the dawn up out of its crested throat; no watchful dog breaks the silence, nor the goose, sharper of hearing than dogs.
sentences.n: The cock is named by description and not by name — vigil ales ... cristati oris, “the wakeful bird of the crested mouth”. sagacior is the comparative of sagax, keen of scent or of hearing, with canibus as ablative of comparison: the goose kept as a watch-animal at Rome, quicker than a dog to raise the alarm.

sentences.t:
Non fera, non pecudes, non moti flamine rami
humanaeve sonum reddunt convicia linguae:
sentences.l: No wild beast, no cattle, no branches stirred by a breeze, no brawlings of the human tongue give back a sound:
sentences.i: No wild animal, no herd, no branch moved by a breath of air, no human squabbling gives back any sound:
sentences.n: convicia is loud abusive noise — quarrelling, jeering — so the last item on the list is not human speech in general but the racket people make with it. reddunt sonum, “give back a sound”, is the language of echo: the place returns nothing. Three non and then a -ve pile the negatives up before the verb arrives.

sentences.t: muta quies habitat;
sentences.l: mute quiet dwells there;
sentences.i: a silent stillness lives there;
sentences.n: Three words close the catalogue of what is absent by naming the one thing present. habitat makes quies the tenant of the cave, the occupant of a house that has no door and no doorkeeper.

sentences.t:
saxo tamen exit ab imo
rivus aquae Lethes, per quem cum murmure labens
invitat somnos crepitantibus unda lapillis.
sentences.l: yet out of the rock's depth there comes a stream of Lethe's water, through which the wave, sliding with a murmur, invites sleeps with its clicking pebbles.
sentences.i: and yet from the foot of the rock a stream of Lethe's water runs out, and the current sliding through it with a murmur, its pebbles clicking, invites sleep.
sentences.n: aquae Lethes keeps the Greek genitive of Lethe, the underworld river of forgetting. somnos is plural, sleeps, one for each sleeper. The murmur is the single exception to the silence just catalogued, and it is the one sound that wakes nobody.

sentences.t:
Ante fores antri fecunda papavera florent
innumeraeque herbae, quarum de lacte soporem
nox legit et spargit per opacas umida terras.
sentences.l: Before the cave's doors fertile poppies bloom, and herbs beyond counting, from whose milk dewy Night gathers drowsiness and sprinkles it over the shadowed lands.
sentences.i: In front of the cave's doorway grow poppies heavy with seed and herbs past counting, and from their milk dewy Night gathers sleep and scatters it over the darkened earth.
sentences.n: de lacte is the milky sap of the poppy — the opium the plant really yields — described as a crop that Night harvests. umida agrees with nox and not with terras: it is the dew-bearing night. legit is “gathers, picks” and spargit “sprinkles”, and the two verbs together make Night a farmer working at the door.

sentences.t: Ianua nec verso stridores cardine reddit:
sentences.l: Nor does the door give back creakings when the hinge is turned:
sentences.i: No door grates on its hinge as it turns:
sentences.n: verso cardine is an ablative absolute — “the hinge having been turned” — where English wants “as it turns”. reddit picks up the reddunt of 601: the whole cave gives nothing back. Some editions print ne ... reddat, which makes the line a wish that the door should not creak; Magnus prints nec ... reddit, a statement that it does not.

sentences.t: nulla domo tota, custos in limine nullus.
sentences.l: none in the whole house, no watchman on the threshold.
sentences.i: there is no door in the whole house, and no doorkeeper at the threshold.
sentences.n: The line has no verb, and nulla has no noun of its own: both are carried over from the line before, “no door in the whole house”. domo tota is a bare ablative of place without a preposition. Some editions supply est; Magnus leaves the line without it.

sentences.t:
At medio torus est ebeno sublimis in antro,
plumeus, unicolor, pullo velamine tectus:
sentences.l: But in the middle of the cave there is a raised couch of ebony, feather-filled, of a single colour, covered with a dark spread:
sentences.i: But in the middle of the cave stands a high couch of ebony, stuffed with feathers, all of one colour, covered with a dark spread:
sentences.n: ebeno is ablative of material, ebony, the blackest wood the Romans knew. unicolor says only that nothing varies the colour; pullo then names it, the dark grey-black of mourning cloth. Some editions read atricolor, “black-coloured”, which states outright what unicolor leaves to be inferred.

sentences.t: quo cubat ipse deus membris languore solutis.
sentences.l: on which the god himself lies, his limbs loosened by heaviness.
sentences.i: and on it the god himself lies, his limbs slack with drowsiness.
sentences.n: membris languore solutis is an ablative absolute, “with his limbs undone by heaviness”; quo is “on which”, the couch. The same noun and participle come back at 648, molli languore solutus, when he sinks down again — his appearance is closed exactly as it was opened.

sentences.t:
Hunc circa passim varias imitantia formas
somnia vana iacent totidem, quot messis aristas,
silva gerit frondes, eiectas litus harenas.
sentences.l: Around him, here and there, lie empty dreams imitating shapes of every kind, as many as the harvest has ears of grain, the wood bears leaves, the shore has sand thrown up on it.
sentences.i: All round him lie empty dreams, copying every kind of shape, as many as the harvest has ears of wheat, the forest leaves, the beach grains of washed-up sand.
sentences.n: Hunc circa is the preposition standing after the word it governs, “around him”. One verb, gerit, serves all three limbs of the comparison, and the first and third have to borrow it. eiectas is the participle of eicio: sand thrown up by the sea, which is what a beach is made of.

sentences.t:
Quo simul intravit manibusque obstantia virgo
somnia dimovit, vestis fulgore reluxit
sacra domus, tardaque deus gravitate iacentes
vix oculos tollens iterumque iterumque relabens
summaque percutiens nutanti pectora mento,
excussit tandem sibi se;
sentences.l: As soon as the maiden entered there and pushed apart with her hands the dreams in her way, the sacred house shone with the blaze of her robe, and the god, hardly lifting his drooping eyes in his slow heaviness, and slipping back again and again, and striking the top of his chest with his nodding chin, at last shook himself out of himself;
sentences.i: The moment the maiden stepped in and pushed the crowding dreams aside with her hands, the holy house lit up with the blaze of her robe; and the god, barely raising his drooping eyes in his slow torpor, sinking back again and again, his nodding chin knocking against the top of his chest, at last shook himself free of himself;
sentences.n: excussit ... sibi se, “he shook himself out of himself”, is the point the whole long sentence is built to reach, with the dative sibi naming what he is being shaken loose from. iacentes oculos are eyes that lie down — the lids will not stay up. The doubled iterumque iterumque and the chin dropping onto the chest keep the waking physical and slow.

sentences.t:
cubitoque levatus,
quid veniat (cognovit enim), scitatur. At illa:
sentences.l: and, raised on his elbow, he asks why she comes (for he recognised her). But she:
sentences.i: and, propping himself on an elbow, he asked what she had come for — he knew her — and she answered:
sentences.n: scitatur is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, “he asks”; quid veniat is an indirect question with the subjunctive. The parenthesis cognovit enim saves the time introductions would take, which matters for a god who is not going to stay awake long.

sentences.t:
“Somne, quies rerum, placidissime, Somne, deorum,
pax animi, quem cura fugit, qui corpora duris
fessa ministeriis mulces reparasque labori,
sentences.l: “Sleep, rest of all things, gentlest, Sleep, of the gods, peace of the mind, whom care flees, you who soothe bodies wearied by hard duties and make them new again for labour,
sentences.i: “Sleep, the rest of all things, Sleep, gentlest of the gods, peace of the mind, the one that care runs from, you who soothe bodies worn out by hard service and build them up again for work,
sentences.n: The vocative Somne is said twice in 623, at the head of the line and again just before its last word, with placidissime ... deorum, “gentlest of the gods”, pulled apart between the two. In quem cura fugit, care is the subject and Sleep the object: worry runs away from him, so where he is there is none. reparas ... labori has a dative of purpose — the rest is restored for the sake of the next day's work.

sentences.t:
somnia, quae veras aequent imitantia formas,
Herculea Trachine iube sub imagine regis
Alcyonen adeant simulacraque naufraga fingant.
Imperat hoc Iuno.”
sentences.l: bid dreams, which imitating may match true shapes, go to Alcyone in Herculean Trachis under the likeness of her king, and fashion shipwrecked likenesses. Juno orders this.”
sentences.i: give the order that dreams, which can match true shapes by copying them, go to Alcyone in Hercules' Trachis wearing her king's likeness and take on the look of a drowned man. This is Juno's command.”
sentences.n: iube ... adeant ... fingant again puts the ordered verbs straight into the subjunctive with no ut, as at 587. aequent imitantia is “match by imitating”: the participle carries the method, the verb the result. Herculea Trachine names the city by Hercules, who died on the mountain above it, and Iris ends on the one word that makes refusal impossible, Iuno. naufraga is an adjective on simulacra: the phantoms are themselves shipwrecked, not pictures of a wreck. Some editions read imitamine, “by imitation”, for imitantia.

sentences.t:
Postquam mandata peregit,
Iris abit (neque enim ulterius tolerare soporis
vim poterat), labique ut somnum sensit in artus,
effugit et remeat per quos modo venerat arcus.
sentences.l: After she had carried out her orders, Iris goes off — for she could bear the force of the drowsiness no longer — and when she felt sleep sliding into her limbs, she flees and returns along the bow by which she had just come.
sentences.i: Her errand delivered, Iris left — she could not stand the weight of the drowsiness any longer — and the moment she felt sleep sliding into her limbs she fled, going back along the rainbow she had just come by.
sentences.n: per quos ... arcus is a relative folded inside its own clause, “along which she had lately come”: the arch of 590. labi is an infinitive with somnum as its accusative subject after sensit, “felt sleep glide”. The tenses slide about — abit, effugit and remeat present against the past peregit, poterat and sensit — and the mixture keeps the exit quick. effugit looks as though it could be the perfect, but the first foot of 632 is a dactyl, so the u is short and the verb is present.

sentences.t:
At pater e populo natorum mille suorum
excitat artificem simulatoremque figurae
Morphea:
sentences.l: But the father rouses out of the crowd of his thousand sons the artificer and counterfeiter of shape, Morpheus:
sentences.i: But the father woke, out of his crowd of a thousand sons, Morpheus, the craftsman and counterfeiter of shape:
sentences.n: pater is Somnus, and the thousand sons are the dreams. artificem simulatoremque figurae stand in apposition and take up the rest of 634, so that the skill is fully stated before the name arrives at the head of 635. The name itself is built on the Greek for form, morphe, which is what figurae says in Latin.

sentences.t:
non illic quisquam sollertius alter
exprimit incessus vultumque sonumque loquendi.
sentences.l: no other there brings out more cleverly walks and face and the sound of speaking.
sentences.i: no one else there reproduces more skilfully the way a man walks, his face, the sound of his speech.
sentences.n: exprimit is “presses out”, the verb of a mould taking an impression, which is exactly what Morpheus does to a person. incessus is fourth-declension accusative plural, gaits, ways of walking. Some editions read illo, “more skilfully than he”, making the comparison explicit; Magnus's illic is “there”, in the cave.

sentences.t:
Adicit et vestes et consuetissima cuique
verba;
sentences.l: He adds too the clothes and the words most habitual to each man;
sentences.i: He adds the clothes as well, and the words each man most often uses;
sentences.n: cuique is dative with consuetissima, the turns of phrase habitual to each particular person. The superlative does a lot of work: not a man's words in general but the ones he cannot help saying.

sentences.t:
sed hic solos homines imitatur, at alter
fit fera, fit volucris, fit longo corpore serpens:
sentences.l: but he imitates human beings only, while another becomes a wild beast, becomes a bird, becomes a snake with a long body:
sentences.i: but he copies human beings only; a second becomes a wild beast, becomes a bird, becomes a snake with its long body:
sentences.n: solos homines is the exact limit of Morpheus's competence: people, and nothing else. The triple fit ... fit ... fit performs the change three times in a single line with no connective, and longo corpore is an ablative of description hung on serpens.

sentences.t:
hunc Icelon superi, mortale Phobetora vulgus
nominat.
sentences.l: him the gods above call Icelos, the mortal crowd Phobetor.
sentences.i: the gods above call him Icelos; ordinary mortals call him Phobetor.
sentences.n: Two names for one brother, each in its own half of line 640, with the single verb nominat opening 641 and serving both. Icelos is Greek for “like”, Phobetor for “frightener”: the divine name describes his resemblance, the human name the fear he causes. Phobetora keeps the Greek accusative in -a.

sentences.t:
Est etiam diversae tertius artis
Phantasos:
sentences.l: There is also a third, of a different skill, Phantasos:
sentences.i: There is a third as well, with a different art: Phantasos.
sentences.n: diversae ... artis is a genitive of description wrapped round tertius — a third brother whose craft is of another kind altogether. Phantasos is Greek again, from the verb for appearing: the name says apparition.

sentences.t:
ille in humum saxumque undamque trabemque
quaeque vacant anima, fallaciter omnia transit.
sentences.l: he passes deceitfully into earth and stone and wave and timber and everything that is empty of breath — all of them.
sentences.i: he turns himself deceitfully into earth and stone and water and a beam of wood, and into everything that has no breath in it.
sentences.n: transit in with the accusative is “crosses over into”, the ordinary way of saying a change of shape, and omnia at the end gathers the whole list up again, an accusative in apposition to everything in has governed. quaeque vacant anima is “and the things that are empty of breath”, with anima an ablative of separation after vaco. The three brothers divide the world between them: Morpheus takes people, the second beasts, birds and snakes, and this one everything with no life in it.

sentences.t:
Regibus hi ducibusque suos ostendere vultus
nocte solent, populos alii plebemque pererrant.
sentences.l: These are used to showing their faces by night to kings and commanders; others range through the peoples and the common crowd.
sentences.i: These three appear by night to kings and generals; the rest wander among the nations and the common people.
sentences.n: hi is the three brothers just named, alii the remainder of the thousand. ostendere solent is the plain construction, “are accustomed to show”. pererrant takes populos and plebem as direct objects, the per- of the compound doing the work an English preposition has to do.

sentences.t:
Praeterit hos senior cunctisque e fratribus unum
Morphea, qui peragat Thaumantidos edita, Somnus
eligit:
sentences.l: The elder passes these by, and out of all his brothers Sleep chooses one, Morpheus, to carry through the utterances of Thaumas's daughter:
sentences.i: The old god passed the others over and out of all the brothers chose one, Morpheus, to carry out what the daughter of Thaumas had declared:
sentences.n: qui peragat is a relative clause of purpose: the subjunctive means “to carry out”, not “who carries out”. Thaumantidos is a Greek genitive — Iris, named by her father instead of by her own name. edita, “things uttered”, is from the verb Ceyx will use of himself at 668, fata ... edo. The subject Somnus is held back to the end of 647, after both the object and the purpose clause, so that it lands beside its verb eligit at the turn of the line.

sentences.t:
et rursus molli languore solutus
deposuitque caput stratoque recondidit alto.
sentences.l: and again, loosened by soft heaviness, he both laid his head down and buried it in the deep bedding.
sentences.i: and once more, slack with soft drowsiness, he let his head fall and buried it in the deep bedding.
sentences.n: molli languore solutus repeats the phrase of 612 so that the god drops back exactly as we found him. deposuitque ... stratoque is the doubled -que ... -que, “both ... and”, which will not go into English and is best left as two plain verbs. stratum is the spread bedding, and altum of it is deep rather than high.

sentences.t:
Ille volat nullos strepitus facientibus alis
per tenebras intraque morae breve tempus in urbem
pervenit Haemoniam positisque e corpore pennis
in faciem Ceycis abit sumptaque figura
luridus, exanimi similis, sine vestibus ullis,
coniugis ante torum miserae stetit:
sentences.l: He flies through the darkness on wings that make no rustle, and within a brief space of delay reaches the Haemonian city, and, his feathers laid aside from his body, he goes over into Ceyx's face, and, that shape taken on, sallow, like a man without breath, without any clothing, he stood before the poor wife's bed:
sentences.i: He flew through the dark on wings that made no sound, and in a moment's delay reached the Haemonian city; there he laid his feathers aside, passed into Ceyx's face, and, taking on that shape — sallow, like a corpse, with no clothes on him — stood at the poor wife's bed:
sentences.n: positis ... pennis and sumpta figura are two ablatives absolute doing the work of an English “once he had”. Haemoniam is Thessalian, the region standing for the city. luridus is the yellow-grey of a body brought out of the water, and exanimi similis, “like one without breath”, says plainly what he is imitating. The tenses run present — volat, pervenit, abit — until the perfect stetit stops him at the bed.

sentences.t:
uda videtur
barba viri, madidisque gravis fluere unda capillis.
sentences.l: The man's beard seems wet, and a heavy stream seems to flow from his drenched hair.
sentences.i: His beard looks soaked, and heavy water seems to be running from his sodden hair.
sentences.n: videtur governs both halves: first as a copula with uda, then with the infinitive fluere, whose subject is unda. madidis ... capillis is ablative of source, the water running off the hair. gravis is nominative with unda — the weight is the water's, not an adverb on the verb.

sentences.t:
Tum lecto incumbens, fletu super ora profuso,
haec ait:
sentences.l: Then, leaning over the bed, with weeping poured out over her face, he says this:
sentences.i: Then, bending over the bed, his tears falling across her face, he said:
sentences.n: fletu ... profuso is an ablative absolute with super ora inside it; the face is most naturally hers, since he is leaning over her bed. incumbens takes the dative lecto: the participle leans on the bed. The tears are a strange thing for a dream to have, and 672 comes back to them — he seemed to be shedding real ones.

sentences.t:
“Agnoscis Ceyca, miserrima coniunx?
An mea mutata est facies?
sentences.l: “Do you recognise Ceyx, most wretched wife? Or has my face been changed?
sentences.i: “Do you know Ceyx, poor wife of mine? Or has my face been altered?
sentences.n: Ceyca is the Greek accusative in -a, and he says his own name where he could have said “me”: the dream speaks of Ceyx in the third person to the one woman who has to identify him. miserrima coniunx is vocative. an introduces the second half of a double question, “or is it that ...”.

sentences.t:
Nunc respice! nosces
inveniesque tuo pro coniuge coniugis umbram.
sentences.l: Now look at me! You will know me, and you will find, in place of your husband, your husband's shade.
sentences.i: Look at me now: you will know me, and instead of your husband you will find your husband's ghost.
sentences.n: tuo pro coniuge coniugis umbram sets the same noun down twice running in two cases, coniuge and then coniugis, husband against husband's shade, and the whole loss is the difference between the cases. nosces and invenies are futures with no object expressed for the first: she will recognise, and only then find out what it is she has recognised.

sentences.t: Nil opis, Alcyone, nobis tua vota tulerunt:
sentences.l: Your prayers brought us nothing of help, Alcyone:
sentences.i: Your prayers brought us no help at all, Alcyone:
sentences.n: nil opis is a partitive genitive, “nothing of aid”. nobis is a plural used of himself alone, and he keeps it up in occidimus in the next line. The vota are the vows she was making at the altars of 584, and the answer is that they bought nothing.

sentences.t: occidimus! Falso tibi me promittere noli!
sentences.l: we have gone down! Do not falsely promise me to yourself!
sentences.i: I am dead! Stop promising yourself I will come back!
sentences.n: occidimus is the plural for one man again, “I have fallen”, the verb of a man going under. noli with the infinitive is the ordinary negative command. falso is the adverb, and tibi me promittere is “to promise me to yourself”, to keep telling yourself he is on his way.

sentences.t:
Nubilus Aegaeo deprendit in aequore navem
auster et ingenti iactatam flamine solvit,
oraque nostra, tuum frustra clamantia nomen,
implerunt fluctus.
sentences.l: The cloud-bringing south wind caught the ship on the Aegean sea and with a huge blast broke it apart as it was tossed, and the waves filled our mouth, which was calling your name in vain.
sentences.i: The south wind, thick with cloud, caught the ship out on the Aegean, tossed it and broke it up in one huge blast, and the waves filled my mouth as it called your name for nothing.
sentences.n: Nubilus ... auster is split over the line-break, the adjective opening 663 and its noun opening 664, with the whole disaster set down between them. iactatam agrees with navem: the ship was being thrown about as it was broken. ora nostra is the plural for one man again, and the mouth calling and the water filling it are put inside a single clause.

sentences.t:
Non haec tibi nuntiat auctor
ambiguus, non ista vagis rumoribus audis:
sentences.l: It is no uncertain informant who reports this to you; you are not hearing these things by roving rumours:
sentences.i: No unreliable messenger is bringing you this; you are not hearing it by rumour going the rounds:
sentences.n: auctor is an authority, the man who stands behind a report; ambiguus is held over to the head of 667, so the doubt arrives a line after the informant does. haec and ista are set against each other, haec what he is telling her now, ista what would have come from somebody else. The double non is a witness establishing his own standing.

sentences.t: ipse ego fata tibi praesens mea naufragus edo.
sentences.l: I myself, here in person, shipwrecked, declare my own fate to you.
sentences.i: I am telling you my own end myself, standing here, drowned.
sentences.n: Four words pile up on the speaker — ipse, ego, praesens, naufragus — before the verb arrives. edo is “give out, declare”, the verb whose participle was edita at 647, where Iris's orders were the thing declared. praesens means present in person, which is the one thing a dream is not.

sentences.t:
Surge, age, da lacrimas lugubriaque indue nec me
indeploratum sub inania Tartara mitte.”
sentences.l: Rise, come, give tears and put on mourning clothes, and do not send me unwept beneath empty Tartarus.”
sentences.i: Get up, come, weep for me, put on mourning, and do not send me down to the empty underworld unmourned.”
sentences.n: lugubria is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, mourning clothes, and indue takes it as its object with no preposition. indeploratum, “unwept-over”, is one of the negative compounds Latin makes easily and English cannot; the whole purpose of the visit is inside that word. nec ... mitte is the bare negative imperative, beside the noli ... promittere of 662.

sentences.t:
Adicit his vocem Morpheus, quam coniugis illa
crederet esse sui:
sentences.l: Morpheus adds to these a voice which she would believe to be her husband's:
sentences.i: Morpheus added to all this a voice she would take for her husband's:
sentences.n: quam ... crederet is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive: the kind of voice she would believe. coniugis ... sui is the genitive after esse, “to be her husband's”. Ovid keeps the name Morpheus out of the whole speech and puts it back only here, when the illusion is being described from outside it.

sentences.t:
fletus quoque fundere veros
visus erat, gestumque manus Ceycis habebat.
sentences.l: He had seemed also to pour out true tears, and he had the gesture of Ceyx's hand.
sentences.i: He seemed, too, to be shedding real tears, and his hand moved as Ceyx's did.
sentences.n: visus erat with the infinitive fundere is “he had seemed to shed”. veros is the difficulty of the line: the tears of a false shape are real tears, and that is what makes the dream work. quoque here is the plain adverb “also”, not the trap quo-que, “and with which”, which is spelt the same. gestum manus is the movement of the hand, a mimic's detail.

sentences.t:
Ingemit Alcyone, lacrimas movet atque lacertos
per somnum, corpusque petens amplectitur auras
exclamatque “mane! quo te rapis? ibimus una!”
sentences.l: Alcyone groans, and moves tears and arms in her sleep, and, reaching for his body, embraces the air, and cries out, “Stay! where are you tearing yourself off to? We shall go together!”
sentences.i: Alcyone groaned and, still asleep, stirred up tears and arms together; reaching for his body she took hold of nothing but air, and cried out, “Stay! where are you rushing off to? We will go together!”
sentences.n: lacrimas movet atque lacertos yokes one verb to two objects that have nothing in common, tears and arms, and English has to strain to keep them in the same phrase. per somnum is “through her sleep”, all of it done asleep. quo te rapis is “where are you carrying yourself off to”, the reflexive of a violent verb. Some editions read lacrimans motatque, “weeping, she keeps moving her arms”, which removes the yoking altogether.

sentences.t:
Voce sua specieque viri turbata soporem
excutit et primo, si sit, circumspicit, illic,
qui modo visus erat:
sentences.l: Startled by her own voice and by the look of her husband, she shakes off her sleep and first looks round to see whether he is there, the one who had just now been seen:
sentences.i: Shaken by her own cry and by the sight of her husband, she threw off sleep and first looked around to see whether he was there, the man she had just seen:
sentences.n: soporem excutit uses the verb of the god's excussit ... sibi se at 621: he shook himself off, she shakes sleep off. si sit is an indirect question, “whether he is”, in the subjunctive — the question she is putting to herself. turbata agrees with her and has two ablatives of cause, her own voice and the shape of the man.

sentences.t:
nam moti voce ministri
intulerant lumen.
sentences.l: for the servants, stirred by her voice, had brought in a light.
sentences.i: for her servants, roused by her cry, had brought a lamp in.
sentences.n: moti voce is a participle with an ablative of cause. The pluperfect intulerant slips a fact in behind the action: the light was already in the room when she looked, which is why looking was possible at all. lumen is the lamp as much as the light it gives.

sentences.t:
Postquam non invenit usquam,
percutit ora manu laniatque a pectore vestes
pectoraque ipsa ferit, nec crines solvere curat:
sentences.l: After she does not find him anywhere, she strikes her face with her hand and tears her clothes away from her breast and beats the breast itself, and does not trouble to loosen her hair:
sentences.i: When she could not find him anywhere she struck her face with her hand, tore the clothes from her breast and beat the breast itself, and did not stop to unbind her hair —
sentences.n: These are the fixed gestures of Roman mourning: the face struck, the clothes torn, the breast beaten, the hair let down. nec crines solvere curat says she skips the last of them, and the next word, scindit, says what she does instead. invenit is the present, not the perfect it could be spelt as: the fifth foot of 680 is a dactyl and needs a short e — a historic present after postquam, where prose would put the perfect.

sentences.t:
scindit et altrici, quae luctus causa, roganti
“nulla est Alcyone, nulla est!” ait.
sentences.l: she tears it, and to her nurse, who asks what the cause of the grief is, she says “Alcyone is nothing, nothing at all!”
sentences.i: she tore it, and to the nurse who asked what the grief was for she said, “There is no Alcyone any more, none!”
sentences.n: nulla est Alcyone is harder than “she is dead”: nulla is “no one, nothing”, and she says it of herself, by name, in the third person. quae luctus causa has no verb — “what the cause of the grief [is]”, with sit left out. altrici is dative and goes with roganti, the nurse who reared her.

sentences.t:
“Occidit una
cum Ceyce suo! Solantia tollite verba!
sentences.l: “She has died together with her own Ceyx! Take your comforting words away!
sentences.i: “She died along with her own Ceyx! Take your comforting words away!
sentences.n: She goes on speaking of herself in the third person, and occidit is the verb Ceyx used of himself at 662. Ceyce is the Greek ablative in -e. tollite is an order to the household: not “stop comforting me” but “carry the words off”, as though they were things being brought into the room.

sentences.t:
Naufragus interiit! Vidi agnovique manusque
ad discedentem cupiens retinere, tetendi.
sentences.l: He died shipwrecked! I saw him and knew him, and, longing to hold him back, I stretched out my hands to him as he went away.
sentences.i: He died in the wreck! I saw him, I knew him, and I put out my hands to him as he went, wanting to keep him.
sentences.n: Vidi agnovique are two bare perfects with no object expressed; English has to supply “him” twice. ad discedentem is a participle used as a noun, “to the one departing”. cupiens retinere puts the wanting and the failing inside one phrase. manusque ... tetendi is split from one line-end to the next, the hands closing 686 and the reaching closing 687.

sentences.t:
Umbra fuit, — sed et umbra tamen manifesta virique
vera mei!
sentences.l: It was a shade — but a shade even so, plain to see, and a true one of my husband!
sentences.i: It was a ghost — but a ghost even so, plain to see, and truly his!
sentences.n: The archive prints a comma and a dash together at Umbra fuit, —, which is the edition's own pointing for the correction she makes to herself. sed et ... tamen doubles the concession, “but even so ... all the same”. manifesta and vera are both nominative with umbra, and viri ... mei, split round vera, is the genitive they hang on: a shade of my husband, and a true one.

sentences.t:
Non ille quidem, si quaeris, habebat
adsuetos vultus, nec quo prius, ore nitebat:
sentences.l: He did not, to be sure, if you ask, have his familiar face, nor did he shine with the face he had before:
sentences.i: No, if you ask me, he did not have the face I knew, nor the brightness of the face he used to have:
sentences.n: si quaeris is an aside to the nurse, “if you want to know”. quo prius has lost both its noun and its verb — “[nor did he shine] with [the face] with which [he shone] before” — and ore, kept back until after the relative clause, supplies the noun that clause needs. adsuetos is the old unassimilated spelling of assuetus, kept as the edition prints it and not a fault.

sentences.t:
pallentem nudumque et adhuc umente capillo
infelix vidi.
sentences.l: Unhappy, I saw him pale and naked and with his hair still dripping.
sentences.i: I saw him — wretched as I am — pale, naked, his hair still wet.
sentences.n: Two accusatives and an ablative of description hang on vidi, which is held to the last: pallentem, nudum, umente capillo. infelix is nominative and agrees with the speaker, not with what she sees — she calls herself unhappy in the middle of describing him. The three details answer 654 and 656 exactly: sallow, unclothed, dripping.

sentences.t:
Stetit hoc miserabilis ipse
ecce loco!” (et quaerit, vestigia siqua supersint)
“Hoc erat, hoc, animo quod divinante timebam,
et ne me fugeres, ventos sequerere, rogabam.
sentences.l: He stood in this place, look, this one, pitiable as he was!” — and she looks whether any footprints are left — “This was it, this, what I feared with my mind foretelling it, and I begged you not to run from me, not to follow the winds.
sentences.i: He stood right here, look, in this very place, in that pitiable state!” — and she searches for any footprint left behind — “This was the thing, this, that I dreaded with a mind that foresaw it; and I begged you not to run from me and go after the winds.
sentences.n: ecce is thrown in between the demonstrative and its noun, hoc ... ecce loco, so that the pointing finger interrupts the phrase. The words in brackets are the narrator's and not hers, and siqua supersint is an indirect question after quaerit. animo divinante is an ablative of means with a participle, “with a mind that was foretelling it” — the mind is the instrument of her fearing, not an absolute. ne ... fugeres, sequerere is one negative purpose after rogabam covering both verbs, and sequerere is the alternative second-person ending for sequereris. Some editions read ipso, which attaches “this very” to the place rather than to him.

sentences.t:
At certe vellem, quoniam periturus abibas,
me quoque duxisses!
sentences.l: But at least I would wish, since you were going away to die, that you had taken me too!
sentences.i: But at least I wish — since you were going away to your death — that you had taken me with you!
sentences.n: vellem is a potential subjunctive, “I could wish”, and duxisses a pluperfect subjunctive for the wish that can never now be granted. periturus is the future participle of pereo, “about to perish”: she puts the outcome back into the moment of departure, which is how she sees it now. quoque is the adverb again, “me too”.

sentences.t:
Multum fuit utile tecum
ire mihi:
sentences.l: It would have been very good for me to go with you:
sentences.i: It would have done me a great deal of good to go with you:
sentences.n: Latin puts the plain indicative fuit where English needs “would have been”: with words of advantage the fact is stated flat and the unreality is left to the situation. tecum ire is the subject of fuit utile, and mihi the dative of the person it would have suited. multum is adverbial with utile.

sentences.t:
neque enim de vitae tempore quicquam
non simul egissem, nec mors discreta fuisset.
sentences.l: for I would have spent no part of life's span that was not spent together, and death would not have been kept apart.
sentences.i: for there would have been no part of my life I did not live beside you, and death would not have been separate either.
sentences.n: neque ... quicquam non is a double negative that has to be kept double in English: not “nothing together” but “nothing that was not together”. egissem and fuisset are pluperfect subjunctives of the unreal past, carrying on the wish of 696. discreta is from discerno, of two things pulled apart from each other.

sentences.t:
Nunc absens perii, iactor quoque fluctibus absens,
et sine me me pontus habet.
sentences.l: As it is, absent I have perished, absent I am tossed too on the waves, and the sea holds me without me.
sentences.i: As it is, I have died elsewhere; elsewhere I am being tossed on the waves as well; and the sea holds me without me.
sentences.n: absens stands twice in 700, as the second word and as the last, and both times it means away from where the thing is happening. sine me me pontus habet sets the two forms of the pronoun side by side, ablative then accusative: the sea has one of them and not the other. She is speaking of her husband's death as her own throughout.

sentences.t:
Crudelior ipso
sit mihi mens pelago, si vitam ducere nitar
longius et tanto pugnem superesse dolori.
sentences.l: May my own mind be crueller to me than the sea itself, if I strive to draw my life out longer and fight to outlive so great a grief.
sentences.i: Let my own mind be crueller to me than the sea, if I try to spin my life out any longer and struggle to survive a grief this size.
sentences.n: sit is a jussive subjunctive, a curse she lays on herself, and the condition that would earn it is her own survival. pelago is ablative of comparison after crudelior. superesse takes the dative dolori, to be left over after a grief, to outlast it. This is the first statement of what she means to do about the rest of her life, and 704 carries it further.

sentences.t:
Sed neque pugnabo, nec te, miserande, relinquam
et tibi nunc saltem veniam comes, inque sepulcro
si non urna, tamen iunget nos littera:
sentences.l: But I shall not fight, nor shall I leave you, pitiable one, and now at least I shall come to you as your companion, and in the tomb, if not an urn, still the lettering will join us:
sentences.i: But I will not fight it; I will not leave you, poor man; now at least I will come to you as your companion, and in the tomb, if no urn joins us, the inscription will:
sentences.n: comes is a noun in apposition to the subject, “I shall come as a companion”, and not an adverb. littera is the writing on the tomb, the names cut in the stone; urna is the jar the ashes go in, which she takes to be out of reach since he drowned at sea. miserande is a vocative gerundive, “you who must be pitied”, and it is her word for him twice in this scene, here and at 728.

sentences.t:
si non
ossibus ossa meis, at nomen nomine tangam.”
sentences.l: if not bones with my bones, still I shall touch name with name.”
sentences.i: if I cannot touch your bones with mine, at least I shall touch name with name.”
sentences.n: The one verb tangam serves both halves and is held to the very end: “if not [shall I touch your] bones with my bones, at least I shall touch name with name”. Each half sets the same noun twice in two cases, ossibus ossa and nomen nomine, so that the touching is done by the grammar as much as by the sense. The names are the two cut on the tomb of the line before.

sentences.t:
Plura dolor prohibet, verboque intervenit omni
plangor, et attonito gemitus a corde trahuntur.
sentences.l: Grief forbids more, and beating of the breast comes between every word, and groans are dragged out of her thunderstruck heart.
sentences.i: Grief will not let her say more; the beating of her breast breaks in on every word, and groans are dragged out of her stunned heart.
sentences.n: plangor is the noise of mourning, the blows on the breast and the cry that goes with them, not silent grief. intervenit takes the dative verbo ... omni, “comes between every word”. attonito is “thunderstruck”, a mind hit by a blow from outside, and trahuntur is passive: the groans are dragged out of her rather than uttered by her.

sentences.t:
Mane erat, egreditur tectis ad litus et illum
maesta locum repetit, de quo spectarat euntem.
sentences.l: It was morning; she goes out from the house to the shore and, in mourning, seeks again that place from which she had watched him going.
sentences.i: It was morning. She left the house for the shore and went sadly back to the place from which she had watched him go.
sentences.n: spectarat is the syncopated pluperfect for spectaverat, normal in verse and not a fault in the text. egreditur is deponent, active in sense, and tectis is an ablative of place from which with no preposition. illum ... locum is split across the line-break, the demonstrative left hanging at the end of 710 and its noun arriving after maesta in 711.

sentences.t:
Dumque moratur ibi, dumque “hic retinacula solvit,
hoc mihi discedens dedit oscula litore” dicit,
quae dum tota locis (s. dumque notata oculis) reminiscitur acta fretumque
prospicit:
sentences.l: And while she lingers there, and while she says “here he loosed the cables, on this shore he gave me kisses as he left”, while she goes back over all that was done, place by place, and looks out over the strait:
sentences.i: And while she waited there, and said, “here he cast off, on this beach he kissed me goodbye”, and while she went back over everything that had happened, place by place, and looked out over the water:
sentences.n: The archive prints this line as quae dum tota locis (s. dumque notata oculis) reminiscitur acta fretumque: an alternative reading has got into the running text, s. being the apparatus's own abbreviation standing before a variant, so that what is inside the bracket belongs to the apparatus and not to the poem. As printed the line runs to some two dozen syllables and cannot be scanned as a hexameter, while both of the shorter readings scan. We ship it exactly as the archive has it and repair nothing; the translation follows the line with the bracket set aside, quae dum tota locis reminiscitur acta, “while she recalls all that was done, in the places”. The second witness reads dumque notata locis reminiscitur acta fretumque, which takes the bracket's participle and keeps locis, and gives “while she recalls the deeds noted in the places”. reminiscitur is deponent and takes acta as its object.

sentences.t:
in liquida, spatio distante, tuetur
nescio quid quasi corpus, aqua.
sentences.l: in the clear water, with a space standing between, she watches something or other, like a body.
sentences.i: out in the clear water, some distance off, she made out something like a body.
sentences.n: in liquida ... aqua is pulled apart so that the phrase wraps the whole clause: the adjective stands in 715 and the noun arrives only after corpus in 716, with the water round the object exactly as the words are round the sentence. nescio quid is a fixed phrase used as one indefinite pronoun, “something-I-know-not-what”. spatio distante is an ablative absolute, “with the space standing between”.

sentences.t:
Primoque, quid illud
esset, erat dubium;
sentences.l: And at first it was uncertain what that thing was;
sentences.i: At first what it was could not be told;
sentences.n: quid illud esset is an indirect question in the imperfect subjunctive standing as the subject of erat dubium, “what that was, was uncertain”. primo is the adverb “at first”, with -que tacking the sentence on. The uncertainty is the reader's here as much as hers.

sentences.t:
postquam paulum appulit unda,
et, quamvis aberat, corpus tamen esse liquebat,
qui foret, ignorans, quia naufragus, omine mota est
et, tamquam ignoto lacrimam daret, “heu! miser” inquit
“quisquis es, et siqua est coniunx tibi !”
sentences.l: after the wave had driven it a little nearer, and, far off though it was, it was clear that it was a body, not knowing who he was, yet because he was shipwrecked, she was moved by the omen, and, as though she were giving a tear to a stranger, “alas, poor man,” she said, “whoever you are, and if you have a wife!”
sentences.i: after the wave had pushed it a little closer, and it was plain, far off as it was, that it was a body — not knowing who it was, but because the man had drowned, she was moved by the sign, and, as though she were shedding a tear for a stranger, she said, “Poor man, whoever you are — and your wife, if you have one!”
sentences.n: quia naufragus has no verb, “because [he was] shipwrecked”, and it gives the whole reason she is moved: the death is of the kind she now fears. omine is ablative — a drowned stranger is a sign about her own husband, and she reads it as one before she knows anything. foret is an alternative form for esset in the indirect question qui foret. The archive prints a space before the exclamation mark at coniunx tibi !, which is the edition's own typography.

sentences.t:
Fluctibus actum
fit propius corpus;
sentences.l: Driven by the waves the body comes nearer;
sentences.i: Driven on by the waves the body came closer;
sentences.n: fit propius is “becomes nearer”, the verb of becoming used of a change in distance, with propius the comparative adverb. actum is the participle of ago and fluctibus an ablative of means: the sea does the moving, and she only watches.

sentences.t:
quod quo magis illa tuetur,
hoc minus et minus est mentis sua, iamque propinquae
admotum terrae, iam quod cognoscere posset,
cernit:
sentences.l: and the more she gazes at it, the less and less is she her own in mind, and now, brought close to the land near by, now something she could recognise, she sees it:
sentences.i: and the more she looked at it, the less and less she belonged to herself; and now, as it was carried close in to the land, now that it was something she could make out, she saw it:
sentences.n: quo magis ... hoc minus is the correlative pair, “the more ... the less”, with ablatives of measure. minus est mentis sua is the hard phrase: mentis is a genitive of the thing in respect of which, sua the predicate — she is less and less her own where her mind is concerned. quod cognoscere posset is a relative clause of characteristic, “a thing she could recognise”. Some editions read vae for sua, which turns the phrase into a cry.

sentences.t: erat coniunx. “Ille est!”
sentences.l: it was her husband. “He it is!”
sentences.i: it was her husband. “It is he!”
sentences.n: erat coniunx has no pronoun and no flourish: two words for the recognition the whole scene has been moving towards. Ille est is the demonstrative used on its own, “that is the man”, and she does not put the name in until the next sentence, ad Ceyca.

sentences.t:
exclamat et una
ora, comas, vestem lacerat tendensque trementes
ad Ceyca manus “sic, o carissime coniunx,
sic ad me, miserande, redis?” ait.
sentences.l: she cries out and all at once tears her face, her hair, her clothing, and, stretching her trembling hands towards Ceyx, “so, o dearest husband,” she says, “so do you come back to me, pitiable one?”
sentences.i: she cried out and all at once tore her face, her hair, her dress, and reaching her trembling hands towards Ceyx said, “Is this how you come back to me, dearest husband — like this, poor man?”
sentences.n: una is the adverb, “together, all at once”, and agrees with nothing. The one verb lacerat takes three objects, ora, comas, vestem — the mourning gestures of 681 done again now that there is a body to do them over. The doubled sic ... sic is the whole reproach: it is the manner of his return she cannot bear. trementes ... manus is split round ad Ceyca, so the hands reach across the line-break to the name.

sentences.t:
Adiacet undis
facta manu moles, quae primas aequoris undas
frangit et incursus quae praedelassat aquarum.
sentences.l: There lies beside the waves a breakwater made by hand, which breaks the sea's first waves and which tires out beforehand the charges of the waters.
sentences.i: Beside the water lies a breakwater built by hand, which breaks the sea's first waves and wears down the rush of the water before it arrives.
sentences.n: moles is a mass of stone thrown up as a breakwater, and facta manu marks it as human work in a scene that is otherwise all sea and birds. praedelassat is a heavy compound, prae- “beforehand” on delasso, “tire out completely”. The second quae stands after its own object incursus, which is fourth-declension accusative plural.

sentences.t: Insilit huc, mirumque fuit potuisse:
sentences.l: She leaps up onto it, and that she could was a marvel:
sentences.i: She leapt up onto it — and that she could was a wonder:
sentences.n: insilit is “leaps onto”, with huc, “to here”, standing for the breakwater. mirum fuit potuisse has a perfect infinitive as the subject of the impersonal, “that she had been able was astonishing”, and the subject of potuisse is left out. Nothing yet says she has wings; the next word says she was flying.

sentences.t:
volabat
percutiensque levem modo natis aera pennis
stringebat summas ales miserabilis undas.
sentences.l: she was flying, and beating the light air with wings just then born, she was skimming the topmost waves, a bird to be pitied.
sentences.i: she was flying: beating the thin air with wings just then grown, she skimmed the tops of the waves, a bird you would pity.
sentences.n: modo natis is “just now born”, of the wings, and her change is given in that participle and nowhere else here — no announcement and no god at this point; the gods are not brought in until 741, where the two of them are changed together. stringebat is “grazes, brushes”, of just touching a surface in passing. ales miserabilis stands in apposition to the subject: she is called a bird only after we have watched her fly.

sentences.t:
Dumque volat, maesto similem plenumque querellae
ora dedere sonum tenui crepitantia rostro.
sentences.l: And while she flies, her mouth, clattering with its slender beak, gave out a sound like a mourner's and full of complaint.
sentences.i: And as she flew, her mouth, clacking with its thin beak, gave out a sound like a mourner's, full of lament.
sentences.n: dedere is the poetic third-person plural perfect, the same as dederunt; verse uses the shorter -ere ending freely, and ora, neuter plural, is its subject. maesto similem has the dative that similis takes, “like a grieving person”. crepitantia agrees with ora and is the verb of the crepitantibus lapillis at 604: the pebbles clicked in the stream, the beak clacks here.

sentences.t:
Ut vero tetigit mutum et sine sanguine corpus,
dilectos artus amplexa recentibus alis
frigida nequiquam duro dedit oscula rostro.
sentences.l: But when she touched the mute and bloodless body, having embraced the beloved limbs with her new wings, she gave cold kisses, in vain, with her hard beak.
sentences.i: But when she touched the silent, bloodless body, folding the limbs she loved in her new wings, she gave it cold kisses, and for nothing, with her hard beak.
sentences.n: amplexa is the perfect participle of a deponent and so is active in sense, “having embraced”. mutum et sine sanguine puts an adjective and a prepositional phrase in the same slot, both describing the corpse. frigida ... oscula is split round nequiquam duro dedit, so that the futility sits inside the kiss, and duro rostro is what makes the kiss cold: the beak has taken the place of her mouth.

sentences.t:
Senserit hoc Ceyx, an vultum motibus undae
tollere sit visus, populus dubitabat:
sentences.l: Whether Ceyx felt this, or whether he seemed to lift his face by the movements of the water, the people were in doubt:
sentences.i: Whether Ceyx felt it, or only seemed to lift his face because the water moved him, the people could not tell:
sentences.n: senserit ... an ... sit visus is a double indirect question after dubitabat, with both verbs in the subjunctive; the first half has no interrogative word at all, only the subjunctive to mark it as a question. motibus undae is an ablative of cause: the water moves him, he does not move himself. The crowd's doubt is set down so that the next line can settle it.

sentences.t:
at ille
senserat, et tandem superis miserantibus, ambo
alite mutantur.
sentences.l: but he had felt it, and at last, with the gods above pitying them, both are changed into a bird.
sentences.i: but he had felt it, and at last, the gods above taking pity, the two of them are turned into birds.
sentences.n: The pluperfect senserat answers the doubt of the line before flatly: he had. superis miserantibus is an ablative absolute, “with the gods above pitying”. alite is a singular ablative of exchange with mutantur — the pair of them are changed into the one kind of bird, and the singular does for both.

sentences.t:
Fatis obnoxius isdem
tunc quoque mansit amor, nec coniugiale solutum est
foedus in alitibus:
sentences.l: Their love, liable to the same destinies, remained then too, nor was the marriage bond loosed in the birds:
sentences.i: Their love, bound to the same fate, stayed with them even then, and the marriage bond was not dissolved in the birds:
sentences.n: isdem is the edition's spelling of the pronoun, for iisdem, “the same”, and is not a fault to be corrected. obnoxius with the dative fatis is “liable to, at the mercy of”. tunc quoque is “then too”, that is, after the change. coniugiale ... foedus is the language of a marriage contract, laid on two birds.

sentences.t:
coeunt fiuntque parentes,
perque dies placidos hiberno tempore septem
incubat Alcyone pendentibus aequore nidis.
sentences.l: they come together and become parents, and through seven calm days in the winter season Alcyone broods on nests hanging on the sea.
sentences.i: they mate and become parents, and for seven calm days in the winter season Alcyone sits on her nest as it hangs on the water.
sentences.n: coeunt is the plain word for mating and also means simply “come together”, which is what the whole story has been about. dies ... septem is split by placidos hiberno tempore, the number kept back to the line-end. pendentibus ... nidis is dative with incubat, which takes what is brooded on in that case; aequore is a bare ablative of place, “on the sea”. These are the halcyon days.

sentences.t: Tunc iacet unda maris:
sentences.l: Then the water of the sea lies still:
sentences.i: Then the sea's water lies flat:
sentences.n: iacet is “lies down”, the verb used of a body at rest, put here to water that has stopped moving. tunc points back to the seven days of 745, and the four words of calm stand against the wreck Ceyx described at 663 and 664.

sentences.t:
ventos custodit et arcet
Aeolus egressu praestatque nepotibus aequor.
sentences.l: Aeolus keeps the winds under guard and bars them from going out, and furnishes the level sea to his grandchildren.
sentences.i: Aeolus keeps the winds locked up and bars them from coming out, and grants his grandchildren a calm sea.
sentences.n: arcet takes egressu as an ablative of separation, “keeps them from going out” — the same verb Juno used of the polluted hands at 584, arceat aris, at the head of this part. nepotibus is dative: the halcyon chicks are the wind-king's grandchildren, which is to say that Alcyone is Aeolus's daughter, and the calm is a family favour. praestat is “furnishes, makes good”, the word for meeting an obligation.
